Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Aerospace Dynamics Corporation Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, during the question-and-answer session, please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. This event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Global Aerospace Dynamics Corporation's Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are John Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Hargrove, Chief Financial Officer; Patricia Lopez, Chief Operating Officer; Dr. Raj Singh, Chief Technology Officer; Karen Weiss, Chief Strategy Officer; and Tom Bradley, Chief Marketing Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements.

John Reynolds:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning. Global Aerospace Dynamics delivered a solid performance in the third quarter, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across commercial aerospace, defense, and services. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. Today, we'll cover key areas including program margins and cost performance, geopolitical factors influencing defense spending, our capital deployment approach, revenue breakdown by segment, analysis of drivers and headwinds, updates on major programs, and our book-to-bill metrics. We're particularly excited about the recent advancements in our Next-Generation Fighter program and its potential to fuel our future growth through high-margin sustainment and international sales. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily as production rates normalize.

I'll now turn it over to Michael for a deeper dive into our financial results.

Michael Hargrove:
Thank you, John, and good morning. Let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $8.7 billion, representing a 14% increase year-over-year. Our adjusted earnings per share were $7.85. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $12.4 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at $35.5 to $36 billion in revenue and $28.50 to $29.00 in adjusted EPS. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Our specific financial highlights include a gross margin of 22.1%, up 140 basis points year-over-year; operating income of $1.95 billion, reflecting 12% growth; and free cash flow of $1.8 billion for the quarter.

Now, let's drill into our program margins and cost performance analysis for the Aerospace & Defense segment, which represented 72% of our total revenue this quarter at $4.8 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Segment operating margins expanded to 11.2%, a 110-basis-point improvement from 10.1% in Q3 2023 and 40 basis points sequentially from Q2 2024. This marks our sixth consecutive quarter of margin expansion, driven by disciplined cost management, production learning curves on mature fixed-price contracts, and favorable contract mix shifts toward high-volume defense sustainment work.

Breaking it down by key program lines with our Earned Value Management metrics for transparency, across our portfolio of over 150 active programs, we maintained an aggregate Cost Performance Index of 1.05, indicating 5% under-budget performance year-to-date, with a Schedule Performance Index of 1.02. This exceeds our internal target of CPI 1.03 and reflects proactive variance mitigation. Year-to-date Estimate at Completion adjustments were minimal at negative $45 million, or 0.3% of program value, mainly from supplier yield improvements on low-rate initial production lots.

In fighter aircraft programs, which are 28% of segment revenue, our flagship Next-Generation Fighter program delivered margins of 12.8%, up from 11.5% last year. Lot 18 production ramped to 48 aircraft, achieving 92% first-pass yield on wing assemblies through digital twin integration using Siemens NX and PTC Windchill PLM systems. CPI was 1.08, with a $120 million negative cost variance from optimized titanium forging processes at our Fort Worth facility. We absorbed a $25 million EAC hit from inflation on avionics semiconductors, but hedged 70% via long-term agreements with RTX and Honeywell. Internationally, Foreign Military Sales to Israel and Poland added $450 million in high-margin upgrades, supported by supplemental U.S. aid amid regional tensions.

For tanker and mobility platforms, 22% of segment revenue, the KC-50 Stratotanker program hit a milestone with delivery of the 25th U.S. Air Force aircraft, lifting margins to 10.5% from 9.2% year-over-year. CPI was 1.04, driven by 15% reduction in non-recurring engineering costs via additive manufacturing of boom pivot joints, cutting part count by 40% and lead times from 18 to 8 weeks. A $60 million positive variance came from rework efficiencies on fuel systems, though we noted a $30 million schedule stretch on boom refueling envelopes due to USAF cyber hardening upgrades. European demand is robust, with a $2.1 billion firm-fixed-price contract from NATO allies for six aircraft, bolstering our 10-year backlog of $28 billion.

Missiles and precision munitions, 19% of segment revenue, saw margins expand to 13.4%, up 180 basis points, from surge production of Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles. We shipped 1,200 units to meet DoD urgent needs, using automated composite layup lines at our Camden, Arkansas facility. CPI of 1.12 reflected a $95 million underrun from scrap rate reductions to 1.2% via AI-driven controls in partnership with Palantir. Regional tailwinds included $800 million in FMS to Australia and the UK under AUKUS, offsetting U.S. inventory delays. We're addressing solid rocket motor shortages through vertical integration, qualifying a second U.S. supplier by Q1 2025.

Space and ISR systems, 15% of segment revenue, faced headwinds with margins at 9.1% from 10.3% year-over-year, due to a $55 million EAC adjustment on our Orion-derived crewed spacecraft module from NASA propulsion redesigns for Artemis III. CPI dipped to 0.98, but SPI held at 1.01. Positively, our smallsat constellation for NRO achieved 14.2% margins on a $1.2 billion spiral contract, with laser comms reducing SWaP-C by 25%. U.S. Space Force budgets up 8% to $30 billion in FY25 support our $15 billion backlog, complemented by commercial NewSpace like proliferated LEO arrays.

Commercial aviation aftermarket, 16% of segment revenue, rebounded to 8.7% margins, up 90 basis points, as Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 engine overhauls normalized. MRO volumes grew 18% to $650 million, with CPI 1.06 from GE Digital's Predix predictive analytics, cutting downtime 22%. Supply chain inflation at 6% on legacy parts was limited by just-in-time inventory with Triumph Group.

Overarching trends show unit costs falling 7% per doubling of output on mature programs. Inflation averaged 4.2%, hedged via 65% fixed-price subcontracts and COLA clauses on 40% of DoD work. Our Resilient Ecosystem program saved $220 million, dual-sourcing 85% of Tier 1 suppliers and using blockchain for rare earths. U.S. DoD FY25 budget at $886 billion supports 85% of our defense backlog, Indo-Pacific tensions drive 25% Asia-Pacific FMS growth, and Europe post-Ukraine saw 30% munitions and tanker orders. We're derisking China supply chains via friendshoring to Mexico and India.

Technically, digital engineering covers 60% of programs with MBSE, compressing cycles 30%; advanced manufacturing scales Directed Energy Deposition for hypersonics; zero-based budgeting saved $180 million; and sustainability includes hybrid-electric UAVs for DoD climate tech. Our $52 billion backlog, 85% funded, converts at 25% CAGR, prioritizing hypersonics, CCA, and missile defense. Risks like labor shortages are met with 5,000 apprenticeships, positioning for FY25 segment margins of 11.5-12.0%.

Building on that, let's discuss geopolitical factors affecting defense spending, which propelled our 12% year-over-year revenue growth, primarily from missiles and fixed-wing platforms. The security environment is the most volatile since the Cold War, with global military expenditure up 6.8% to $2.44 trillion in 2023 per SIPRI, accelerating to 7-9% CAGR through 2028 from peer threats, flashpoints, and Western deterrence.

In Europe, Russia's invasion of Ukraine has NATO spending at €270 billion, up 16%, with 23 members at 2% GDP. This drives replenishment for our air and missile defense like Patriot PAC-3 MSE to Poland and Germany via FMS. Our European backlog is $45 billion, up 25%, aligned with European Sky Shield against Kinzhal hypersonics and EU's €100 billion strategy, including FCAS sensor fusion.

Indo-Pacific tensions over Taiwan and South China Sea boost INDOPACOM budgets 18% to $22 billion, with China's PLA Navy at 370 ships and DF-17 tests prompting $12 billion HIMARS and PrSM deals with Australia, SM-6 for Japan. APAC revenues up 32% to $2.1 billion, with CCA tech transfers.

Middle East Israel-Hamas and Houthi issues spike counter-UAS and munitions demand; Iron Dome expended 5,000 rounds, accelerating $15 billion FMS for Iron Dome and David's Sling, plus Saudi $3.2 billion. E-7 Wedgetail provides C4ISR.

U.S. FY24 NDAA at $886 billion, FY25 prospects $895-910 billion with Columbia SSBN and B-21. U.S. backlog $142 billion on JADC2.

These de-risk our $210 billion backlog, 65% multi-year, with dual-sourcing titanium and rare earths, $1.2 billion R&D for digital twins and AI sustainment cutting F-35 costs 15%. Geopolitics drives 10-12% organic growth, book-to-bill 1.4x, international sales 28%.

Next, our capital deployment strategy balances shareholder returns with growth. We generated $1.8 billion free cash flow in Q3, on track for $6.2-6.5 billion full-year, with $12.4 billion cash and 1.8x net debt-to-EBITDA. We target 4-5% total shareholder yield, delivering 12% CAGR TSR, outperforming peers.

Dividends are bedrock; Q3 $0.58 per share, 10% hike, full-year $2.32, 42% payout, 2.3% yield, 8-10% growth ahead from $450 million savings in ERP and supply chain.

Buybacks: $850 million Q3, 2.1 million shares at $402 average, YTD $2.3 billion vs. $4 billion authorization. Trades at 18x EV/EBITDA; plan $1 billion quarterly post-FY25 NDAA, seek $5 billion more, 1-2% share reduction.

M&A: $1.7 billion YTD, $1.2 billion AeroPropel for hypersonics, $120 million synergies, 10% accretion, $15 billion market. AUKUS Pillar II, Middle East counter-UAS. Pipeline $10 billion for cyber, autonomy. $800 million internal, $300 million IR&D quantum encryption.

Balance sheet: $4.2 billion revolver, 1.5-2.5x leverage, hedged 85% inflation. Return $5.5 billion FY24, invest $3 billion for mid-teens EPS growth.

Turning to revenue by segment: consolidated $8.7 billion, up 16% YoY, book-to-bill 1.25x, backlog $145 billion.

Commercial Aerospace: $4.2 billion, 48%, +28% YoY, from LEAP-1A/1B ramps, CFM to 1,000+ engines/month. Narrowbody 65%, widebody +22%. North America 55%, Europe 25%, Asia 15% despite COMAC delays. Titanium delays down to 5%; $500 million additive for fan blades, SAF. FY25 25-30% growth.

Defense: $3.1 billion, 36%, +9%, F-35 $1.2 billion +12%, hypersonics +18%. Europe 30% +15% FCAS/Tempest, Middle East +10%. Digital engineering shortens timelines 20%; 8-12% FY25 growth.

Services: $1.4 billion, 16%, +18%, MRO 70% backlog. Commercial +25%, defense +12% F-16/Eurofighter. EMEA 40%, TrueChoice model 40% margins, AI PHM. 15-20% growth.

Now, analysis of revenue drivers and headwinds: drivers 72% growth. Defense $8.2 billion +22% from F-35 Lot 15 95% on-time, hypersonics $450 million ARRW. Commercial $4.9 billion +14%, nacelles +25%, MRO +28%. Space $1.6 billion +32%, ESPA $720 million, Artemis $380 million, eVTOL $150 million.

Headwinds: supply chain GTF delays $250 million, titanium -20%, labor overtime 120 bps. Inflation $180 million offset by pricing. Export controls $100 million, Europe cert delays $220 million, Red Sea +15% freight.

Initiatives: $450 million R&D additive, supply chain center diversifies 65%, SAF liners. Margins 12.5% +150 bps.

Updates on key programs: funded backlog $28.7 billion +12%, 85% milestones hit.

NGAD: Milestone B FY25 track, PDR ahead, AI CCA, LRIP Lot 1 $2.1 billion, first metal cut, 14.5% margins MBSE.

Hypersonics Dark Eagle: 3 flight tests Mach 7+, first production glide body $1.8 billion, ramp 8 to 18 units, Huntsville center, $320 million FMS Australia AUKUS.

MQ-Next: IOC, 42 delivered +35%, 28-hour orbits, $1.2 billion Block 2, 16.2% margins, Saudi $750 million counter-UAS.

GMD EKV: 25th intercept, 20 more $900 million, 4/month, $150 million DEW lasers GPI 2025.

Commercial: 737 MAX/787 $2.4 billion +18%, Airbus $500 million.

$100 billion NGAD/CCA, ITAR exports, AI kill chain, FY25 $849.8 billion DoD.

Book-to-bill overall 1.18x, $2.8 billion bookings vs. $2.4 billion revenue, funded backlog $48.7 billion +14%.

Defense 1.27x, $1.6 billion, F-35 $1.2 billion, hypersonics $450 million, NATO PAC-3, Saudi.

Commercial 0.92x, $780 million, 737 MAX/A320neo, Asia 35%, additive landing gear.

Space & Missiles 1.45x, $620 million, Artemis $500 million, GPI $150 million, AUKUS +30%.

Services 1.10x, $140 million, GE9X/PW1000G 85% utilization.

Balanced portfolio, FY24 1.12-1.15x guide, $15 billion pipeline.

That covers our financial and operational highlights.

Patricia Lopez:
Thank you, Michael. Operationally, we have seen significant improvements in our supply chain management, allowing us to increase production rates on key programs like the Next-Generation Fighter and KC-50. We're investing in automation and digital technologies, including our Resilient Ecosystem program that dual-sourced 85% of Tier 1 suppliers and delivered $220 million in savings through blockchain traceability and friendshoring. This has reduced titanium delays to 5% and scrap rates to 1.2%, enabling ramps like 48 aircraft in Lot 18 and 1,200 missiles shipped.

Dr. Raj Singh:
Thank you, Patricia. On the technology front, we're making significant strides in next-generation propulsion systems and digital engineering. Sixty percent of programs now use MBSE, compressing design cycles 30% and reducing F-35-like flight tests 15%. We've integrated digital twins via Siemens NX, AI process controls with Palantir, and advanced manufacturing like Directed Energy Deposition for hypersonic nozzles and additive for boom joints, targeting 20% cost avoidance. Laser comms cut SWaP-C 25% in smallsats, and hybrid-electric UAVs position us for DoD climate initiatives. These give us a competitive edge in NGAD, hypersonics, and CCA.

Karen Weiss:
Thank you, Raj. From a strategic perspective, we are actively evaluating potential acquisitions like the recent AeroPropel deal to complement our portfolio and expand into hypersonics and counter-UAS, with a $10 billion pipeline targeting 5-7% EPS accretion. We're developing new models for JADC2, autonomy, and international FMS growth under AUKUS and Abraham Accords, diversifying beyond 65% U.S. DoD while leveraging our $210 billion backlog for 10-12% organic growth.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Josh Friedman with RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Josh Friedman:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the program margins expansion, particularly in missiles and any EAC risks ahead?

John Reynolds:
Certainly, Josh. As Michael detailed, margins expanded across the board, with missiles hitting 13.4% from high-volume JASSM-ER shipments and underruns via AI controls. Aggregate CPI 1.05 shows we're under budget, EACs minimal at 0.3%, mitigated by hedging and supplier improvements. Risks like inflation are managed with 65% fixed-price subs, and we see continued expansion to 11.5-12% segment-wide in FY25.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Laura Bennett with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Laura Bennett:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about revenue drivers in commercial aerospace and headwinds from supply chain?

Michael Hargrove:
Laura, commercial drove 28% growth to $4.2 billion from LEAP components and MRO surge, with widebody recovery and Asia aftermarket. Headwinds like GTF delays and titanium were offset by dual-sourcing, limiting impact to 300-400 bps, and our investments in additive manufacturing position us for 25-30% FY25 growth as Boeing and Airbus ramp.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Torres with Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.

Mike Torres:
Regarding the book-to-bill by segment and geopolitical impacts on defense bookings?

Dr. Raj Singh:
Mike, overall 1.18x with defense at 1.27x from F-35 and hypersonics awards, space 1.45x on Artemis and AUKUS. Geopolitics like Ukraine, Indo-Pacific, and Middle East are structural, boosting FMS 22% YoY and backlog to records, with our tech like digital twins ensuring we capture JADC2 and CCA opportunities.

John Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
